Will Manchester United choose the 'easy option' when it comes to Bruno Fernandes' future, just as they did with handing Michael Carrick the permanent job?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United are under new management and need to be under new leadership on the field.

Bruno Fernandes has undeniably been a flickering beacon of brief hope for United in darkening times. He’s been their Player of the Year in five of the last seven seasons, risen to 19th of their greatest scorers with 113 goals, has scored 75 times (24 pens, four free-kicks) and provided 74 assists in 240 Premier League games and is the reigning Footballer of the Year. But it’s undeniably time for the club to face reality, resist the urge to extend a contract which expires next summer and build for the future.

Even taking up the year’s option (unless to increase the player’s transfer fee) would be a retrograde step. Fernandes is 32, slowing up, and not now “best in class, 10 out of 10s” to borrow Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s catchphrase. He is not the most convincing of captains, moans too much and flaps his arms like a fledgling dove attempting to leave the nest.

Fernandes would never, ever be considered one of United’s elite captains in a strong, historic field that includes Sir Bobby Charlton, Roy Keane, Bryan Robson, Steve Bruce, Roger Byrne, Nemanja Vidic and Gary Neville, amongst others.

All are different; Neville was very vocal, Charlton led by example, but were united in their total commitment.

Fernandes’ leadership qualities were brought into question when he openly criticised the tactics of Michael Carrick, effectively undermining him. That may not have been Fernandes’ intention when questioning the tactical approach against Como but it certainly didn’t help Carrick at a time when he needed players standing up to be counted, not standing up to his tactics in public. Such concerns – some of them legitimate – should have been aired in private.

It showed a lack of leadership from Fernandes, a lack of gratitude, too. Fernandes wouldn’t have been named the writers’ Footballer of the Year and the players’ Player of the Year without Carrick reviving United’s fortunes and their No. 8’s form last season.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In receiving the writers’ award in May, Fernandes eulogised about the interim head coach, praising “the amazing job” he did in guiding United into the Champions League and saying Carrick possesses the “great character to become a top manager”.

Such an endorsement from such an influential figure at the club, effectively the voice of the dressing-room, undoubtedly contributed to Ineos and the Glazers appointing Carrick to the permanent role.

Bruno’s voice is powerful. That is why it was damaging when he spoke out against Carrick’s tactics. “Lies,” was Bruno’s reaction to some of the interpretation of his words but mud stuck.

Carrick questioned individuals’ running stats – without naming Fernandes – and then dropped him for the game against Bournemouth. United need real leaders. In fairness to Fernandes, there are plenty of stories of the good work he does behind the scenes.

Who would inherit the armband in the unlikely event that Carrick’s successor, Mauricio Pochettino, was brave and looked to the future? Matthijs de Ligt, an Ajax captain at 18, would be a strong contender were it not for his back problems. Senne Lammens represents United admirably on and off the field, and was one of only two who emerged with reputation intact from Anfield.

The other was Kobbie Mainoo. It might seem a leap of faith in one so young, still only 21, but Mainoo could perform the duties until a more experienced leader was recruited by the club that once bought Keane, Bruce, Vidic etc. (All of this is a reminder of United’s need to buy leaders, powerful characters as well as good players).

Mainoo’s one of the few deserving of his place currently. He’s also an academy graduate, a local lad, and a link to great home-grown generations. Fans would love that re-affirmation of United’s identity. It would be quite a statement by Pochettino.

Mainoo has only minimal captaincy experience against Bayern Munich in 2017 (as a kid) and successfully with England Under-19s in 2023. More recently, more pertinently, Mainoo acted like a leader against Roma on November 3 when others were losing their discipline.

It’s still too early, of course, and Mainoo is still developing but he could do the honours on a temporary basis in the unlikely event that United cut the cord with Fernandes. But a recruitment department incapable of making strong decisions and buying “best in class” – they were not in the running when Elliot Anderson and Morgan Rogers were available in the summer - may be tempted to go for the easy option of keeping Fernandes, rather than step into a new era.

Henry Winter is one of football's most popular and respected writers. Previously the Chief Football Writer for The Times and a Football Correspondent for The Daily Telegraph, his work now primarily features on his Substack. He has also lauched his own podcast 'The Winter View'

#935. The Mona Lisa Lottery

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gretchen Tessmer is an attorney/writer based in the US/Canadian borderlands of Northern New York.

There’s a bell ringing in the Underground.

The copper-line page phone in Shaft #4 is going off, but it takes a minute for any of the miners to notice. They’re too busy dealing with a tunnel collapse and subsequent break in the geothermal line servicing Sectors 51–57.

It’s late morning, as measured by the water clocks and those who swear by them. It’s midnight, as determined by the Moon and stars, cavorting a few thousand feet above their heads. But the oldest miner on this crew is 60, which is about 30 years too young to remember stars or moons, or appreciate the difference between morning and night.

This is one reason why the Mona Lisa Lottery, so loved by the old-timers, fails to stir up the same excitement it used to. Too intent on repairs, the miners forget that the annual drawing is scheduled for today.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Eventually, the ringing registers and curiosity calls them away from their work. Headlamps bob up and down in the dark. The sound of axes and drills drops off sharply, save for one stubborn miner still working, right below a rock face chiselled with the encouraging-but-long-false words: This Way Out.

They gather round the ringer box and the foreman hushes them before pressing the phone tight to one ear, cupping his free hand over the other. Every noise echoes tenfold in the tunnels, and the foreman has to ask the voice on the other end to repeat themselves.

“Abel?” the foreman repeats. “Are you sure?”

A few miners huff wry laughs at the name, muttering, “Of course it’s him.”

The foreman looks around, failing to find the lucky winner among his workers, “Well, where is he?”

A couple outstretched thumbs and jerks of the head give the foreman his answer, unmistakably directed towards the only pickaxe still singing in the dark.

No one can opt out of the Mona Lisa Lottery. No one can give away their ticket to someone else.

But Abel’s tempted to decline the honour. He’s got work to do. And climbing up 2,000 feet to wait in line with the other winners for hours, all to stare at a square 30-by-21 inches for 5 whole minutes, doesn’t seem like a good use of his time.

It’s only Adèle, the old woman in the cave next door, who convinces him to make the trek upstairs.

Adèle was ten when the evacuations happened. She’s now two months shy of being a proper centenarian. Her mind isn’t as sharp as it used to be. She can’t remember what she had for breakfast, but she remembers the horrors they descended from well enough, all those lines of desperate people sent down below with canned goods, heirloom seeds and not much else.

The treasures preserved from the Old World are few and Abel’s been given the chance to see one of the last. Arguably, the best. If she wasn’t blind as a bat, Adèle might kill him for his ticket. If she didn’t love him like a son, that is.

“Don’t be a fool,” she tells him plainly. “Go see what you’ve been missing.”

The journey to the higher levels snakes up ladders and through tight squeezes, skirting the underbelly of the Safe Zone. There’s a breath of strange breeze up here, not conjured by any air machines. It makes some winners too nervous and they abandon the wait, rushing back down the way they came.

Abel’s not afraid. But he still thinks it’s a waste of time.

Adèle warned him that the wait for the Mona Lisa was just like this. When she was eight, her family waited for two hours just to get a glimpse. It doesn’t make sense to him. He doesn’t understand how a mere painting could be worth the trouble.

He’ll never know. Because that’s not what the Mona Lisa Lottery is all about. Despite the name, Abel’s not queuing for oil paint on a poplar panel.

The Mona Lisa is not in the Underground. They couldn’t waste the limited space. Leonardo’s lady still sits in the crumbling ruins of her museum gallery, her half-smile gone grimmer these days. She’s lonely without visitors. A wild boar passed her way a decade before, searching for truffles in the jungles of the overgrown Louvre. No one’s been by since.

She sighs into her patient smile; she waits with folded hands. Ever the optimist, she thinks her friends may return someday.

#934. Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters for AI race

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."

The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

#933. Whiff of arrogance as Arsenal unexpectedly implode

Arsenal were cruising. This was life on Premier League easy street, but from complete control of this game against Newcastle United, they tossed it away. It was a spectacular, unexpected implosion. They were extremely fortunate to escape with a point.

You cannot switch off away from home in the Premier League and you certainly can never be complacent against a team with Newcastle’s home crowd behind them.

From control to disarray. From looking like champions, Arsenal, who also lost goalkeeper David Raya to a worrying looking injury, rumbled under pressure. To go from dominance to being grateful for a draw, this was a flaky side of the Premier League leaders we have not seen for a while.

“We have lost two points,” said manager Mikel Arteta. “We were exceptional in the first half, the intensity and the quality, we should have been two, three or four goals up.

“When you don’t do that, in the second half you cannot give the opposition belief and you cannot give them goals. We did both. We started to lose duels, second balls, we gave it away.”

Was it arrogance? Did the title-holders start to believe they were simply too good to be hurt or worried by a team with Newcastle’s obvious limitations? It looked like it. The way Arsenal fell apart as soon as the momentum in the game shifted in the home team’s favour in the second half was shocking.

Newcastle were dreadful before the break and managed just one attack before half-time. Perhaps it was all too easy for Arteta’s side. They have become used to ferocious battles on Tyneside, but this was a stroll for 45 minutes. When it turned into a proper test after half-time, though, they folded.

"Absolutely clinical!" Eberechi Eze scores his first Premier League goal of the season to give Arsenal the lead 🔴 https://t.co/34IbZuuJuN

The visitors took a deserved lead, through Eberechi Eze, having barely had to break sweat, but the way they approached the second half was baffling. As soon as Newcastle got in their faces and made it a scrap, Arsenal were bullied, ruffled and rushed into mistakes.

To give the opposition one goal against the run of play can be forgiven, but to do it a second time, when the heat is cranked up, hints at a fragility we no longer thought existed under Arteta.

The first goal came from a blunder by captain Martin Odegaard. It was a lazy, sloppy swing of the leg to try to clear a throw-in and the ball sliced backwards. When it looped into the path of Will Osula, he squared to the unmarked Harvey Barnes who put away the equaliser comfortably.

"Horrendous error!" Harvey Barnes puts Newcastle level 👊 https://t.co/YWrHZPxBIo

It was Newcastle’s first shot on target, but Arsenal’s air of invincibility vanished and the crowd sensed it. Newcastle players responded to the noise, snapping into tackles and pouring forward in numbers, yet the second goal was also an Arsenal gift.

Newcastle deserved it. For half an hour in the second half they were the better side. From the depths of despair, from the apathy and boos of half-time, this was a completely different team.

If this is the vertical football Matthias Jaissle has preached since he arrived in August, Newcastle supporters can buy into it. There was speed, a physicality and a boldness in this second-half performance. It was fun and exciting. It was football played on the front foot. It was what we were promised when the German replaced Eddie Howe.

“That is Newcastle’s DNA, the second half is what we want this team to play like,” said Jaissle. “We knew there would be ups and downs this season, but if we can put that performance together for 90 minutes we can definitely say we are moving in the right direction.”

The problem is, Newcastle have not put a 90-minute performance like this together all season. We have only seen it in flashes and as good as the second half was, we cannot lose sight of the fact the first was abject. Newcastle’s football was aimless, clueless and dysfunctional. One attack before the break, one deflected shot wide is simply not good enough.

The transformation at half-time was unexpected. The substitutes helped; Tino Livramento was a massive upgrade on Amar Dedic at right-back, Jacob Ramsey improved the midfield and Anthony Elanga brought speed and, yes, a vertical threat to their attack.

But Jaissle’s side did not hold on for the win. They had the chances to score a third, but it was their ambition to do so that caused their downfall. Arsenal’s class shone again, passing through the lines to release Noni Madueke.

The winger still had lots to do, but having cut inside, leaving two Newcastle defenders on the ground, his shot squeezed through a crowd and through the arms of goalkeeper Lukasz Hornicek. And it should have been 2-0, 3-0 or 4-0 up, clear.

“And I say we give them belief because we give them a goal, we give them a throw-in that we just give them the ball. We have no structure to control the opposite winger. Bruno Guimarães’s move to Arsenal was one of the most explosive transfers of the summer as Newcastle United’s talisman and captain left a club where he was adored.

As the Brazil international returns to St James’ Park on Saturday evening for the first time since completing his £75m switch in August, the circumstances around his controversial exit are brought back into focus.

Guimarães hurt a lot of people when he forced his way out and while the wounds will heal in time given how brilliant the midfielder was for 4½ years, he can expect a hostile reception.

The 29-year-old was a majestic player for Newcastle, but the way he conducted himself in the summer left supporters feeling betrayed. Telegraph Sport reveals for the first time the events leading up to his Arsenal move, what motivated it and what is behind his inconsistent start at the Emirates.

Arsenal were hoping to tie up transfer business in January - which has been seriously complicated

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal's January transfer plans have been thrown into chaos following an anterior cruciate ligament injury.

The Gunners strengthened over the summer to bring in Ezri Konsa and Bruno Guimaraes in defence and midfield respectively, but with Gabriel Jesus, Gabriel Martinelli and Leandro Trossard all leaving in attack, only Christos Tzolis came into replace the trio.

With Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta needing reinforcements in attack, the window transfer window would have seen the Gunners have a free run at some of their bigger targets – until now.

Over the weekend, Paris Saint-Germain forward Desire Doue was stretchered off against Nice with a suspected ACL rupture.

This is the second time that a PSG attacker has suffered a season-ending injury in the past few weeks, with Khvicha Kvaratskhelia also damaging his ACL against Barcelona in the Champions League earlier this season.

The double-blow leaves the European champions light in attack, with Ousmane Dembele the only remaining recognised senior forward from the past two Champions League-winning campaigns, and the 2025 Ballon d'Or winner supplemented by the likes of Mika Godts, Magnes Akliouche and the 2026 World Cup final scorer, Ferran Torres.

And while much of this has very little to do with the team that PSG beat in last year's Champions League final, Arsenal, both sides have had similar targets on their radar over the past 18 months.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Godts was admired by Arteta before his switch to Ligue 1, as was Torres – while Bournemouth's Eli Junior Kroupi is thought to be a big target in attack this winter for the Gunners, as per TEAMtalk, along with Antonio Nusa.

Julian Alvarez is another big-name forward that both PSG and Arsenal were vying for in the summer, with the Argentine ruling out a move to anywhere other than Barcelona.

January will be a difficult time in N5 for business as it is, given their approach over the summer.

The champions were blown out of the water for a move for Morgan Rogers, valuing him at over £20 million less than what he moved for, while a deal for Bradley Barcola remained a non-starter due to the Frenchman's extortionate price tag.

If Arteta is to bring in a new face midseason, the Gunners may have to break the bank – and with PSG competing with them, that may just complicate things far more than expected.

Arsenal face Borussia Dortmund as Champions League action resumes this week.

Liverpool and Manchester United have never been this far apart, following yet another mauling of the Red Devils

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

“You’re not famous any more,” was one of the many taunts from The Kop aimed at Manchester United as Liverpool romped to a 4-0 win against Maurico Pochettino’s new team.

Of course, the early dismissal of Leny Yoro helped the home side and hindered their relegation zone opponents, but it’s hard to think the result would have been much different if this had been 11 vs. 11 throughout.

Liverpool finished the match having missed six big chances.

Alexander Isak, who was highly impressive in the first half, especially, with his off-the-ball movement and defensive work seemingly improving under Andoni Iraola, had a goal-bound effort blocked by Harry Maguire before the break and blazed a good chance wide in the second half. On another day, the Swede would’ve bagged two.

Bradley Barcola, who is far from a clinical finisher, had several opportunities to score himself or assist another. His pace for the third goal shows where his strengths are but his composure in front of goal is an area of weakness.

"Even the best team in the world playing in these circumstances after eight minutes would concede four goals or even more,” insisted Pochettino post-match.

Maybe he was right, because Liverpool were sensational going forward, their front four connecting superbly, with Florian Wirtz the chief orchestrator. The German is really finding form for Iraola’s side and created an incredible 10 chances in the game - five of them defined as big chances.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That’s the most chances created by a single player in a Premier League game since 2015.

Then there was Rio Ngumoha, the teenager absolutely tormenting Diogo Dalot, and unsurprisingly, completing the most dribbles in the game and having the most touches in the opposition box.

Liverpool ended the game with 60 touches inside Manchester United’s box, 28 shots on goal, and an xG of 4.35 - which is vastly higher than recorded in the 7-0 mauling three years ago (2.91).

That this was the fifth time in five years that Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson Becker had played a game between these sides and won by at least a three-goal margin underlines the chasm between the two north-west rivals.

Alisson has stood in the Liverpool goal for a 7-0, a 5-0, two 4-0s, and a 3-0 victory all since 2021. For Liverpool fans who sat through the nineties, and parts of the noughties, having their dreams shattered by Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United, this is an experience that heals many childhood traumas.

But, as much as the 1990s were a barren decade in Liverpool’s history, they were never as bad as this post-Ferguson United are.

In fact, Liverpool never lost to United by more than a two-goal margin throughout their worst decade in the modern era. A 4-0 reverse at Old Trafford in 2003 and a 3-0 in 2014 are the only two times United have beaten Liverpool by more than two goals since 1969.

In the last 50 years, United’s top scorer in this fixture is Marcus Rashford with seven goals. In that same time, Mo Salah scored 16 and Steven Gerrard nine.

Liverpool weren’t great during the ‘90s and for parts of the ‘00s, but they were at least competitive, especially in these fixtures that mean so much to supporters. United once again crumbled against their main rival, the two teams that have won the league title the joint-most times in English football history.

Even the best team in the world playing in these circumstances after eight minutes would concede four goals or even more.

“Going down with the City,” was another chant from the Liverpool faithful, who enjoyed seeing Iraola give some Jurgen Klopp-like celebrations, albeit much less extravagant, post-match. “Always I enjoy the moment,” said the Spaniard. “I think we owe them (the fans) because we have had much better results away and we want to solve this and want to give them a big win and more to celebrate.”This is a huge win for Iraola, whose Liverpool career has begun well but seen disappointing home results in his first five league games.

With a big win over Man United now under his belt, the confidence is brimming. “I’m pretty sure things are going to be falling into place for the club,” said a buoyed Virgil van Dijk. “It takes a bit of time, when you are new at any profession or any place you work at you need a little bit of time.”

Time is something United don’t have, with only one league win by late November and firmly in the relegation zone.

This game and the situation of both teams, each with new managers but at different stages in their development, truly underlined how Liverpool have managed to avoid the post-Klopp era capitulation that United have been troubled by for the last 13 years.

One club had a successful manager oversee an era of dominance, the other is a successful club with multiple eras of dominance under different managers.

Matt Ladson is the co-founder and editor of This Is Anfield, the independent Liverpool news and comment website, and covers all areas of the Reds for FourFourTwo – including transfer analysis, interviews, title wins and European trophies. As well as writing about Liverpool for FourFourTwo he also contributes to other titles including Yahoo and Bleacher Report. He is a lifelong fan of the Reds.

#929. Any regrets, Mauricio? Man Utd are deep in relegation battle after Anfield farce

The Liverpool fans did not miss a beat. They never do. “Poch is at the wheel,” they goaded as this calamity unfolded. But at the wheel of what, a clown car? The look of thunder on Mauricio Pochettino’s face said it all as he got off to the worst start of any Manchester United manager – or head coach – in 100 years.

The Pochettino bandwagon rolled into town with the usual fanfare of a new era, new belief, new hope; and then the wheels came off, the doors collapsed and the engine exploded. The opening quarter of an hour really was that farcical.

In that time, away to Liverpool of all places, they were 2-0 down, a player down – and down and out. If Pochettino had any uncertainty over the scale of the task ahead of him, there it was laid bare. Of course United had some mitigation. They played almost the entire game with 10 men, but teams have coped with that before and shown far more resistance and resilience. By the time United did that, it was game over. No one expected a quick fix, but come on.

Any regrets, Mauricio? Whatever the salary, he could be forgiven for having a few as he watched on. This is a far cry from being in charge of the United States and watching them roll over Haiti 8-0 on aggregate, as he did last week. If Liverpool had been more ruthless, it could have been 8-0 here.

In the end it was 4-0 – the same scoreline by which Lal Hilditch lost his first game at United, away to Bolton Wanderers in October 1926. Hilditch was a stop-gap player-manager and former central defender Pochettino may well have been tempted to bring himself on, even at the age of 54. He could barely have done worse.

Pochettino, too, can take some responsibility. Eyebrows were certainly raised when he dropped Harry Maguire – who he then had to bring on after 22 minutes – to hand Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in 357 days. De Ligt was then at fault for the first and, arguably, the second goal.

Did the head coach start with a back three or a back four? The players seemed confused. It eventually ended up as a back five.

But this was a collective failing for United. From the top – with director of football Jason Wilcox caught on camera with his head buried in his coat – through the club and out on the pitch. Pochettino is big on building a culture. So he has to abolish the comedy and the chaos and restore credibility.

United are deep in a relegation battle. Have no doubt. Eight points after 11 games means they are currently on target for fewer than 28 points, which is a lower points-per-game total than when they were relegated in 1974.

The work needed at United is monumental. The transfer strategy has been inexplicable, with the decision being to rebuild the attack last year, the midfield this summer and wait until next year to remodel the defence. The folly of that has been exposed by the fact that United have conceded 34 goals already this season, the most in the top five European leagues.

United will argue, with justification, that Leny Yoro’s eighth-minute sending-off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity was harsh given that Alexander Isak appeared to have already lost control of the ball. But what was Yoro thinking as he bundled into the back of the forward? And what was De Ligt doing as he watched on, or lumbered on, after failing to track the run from Ronald Araújo’s ball over the top?

Andoni Iraola had a very clear message for his players ahead of this game: don’t fall into a trap.

It’s remarkable to see Manchester United arrive at Anfield in the bottom three but, to go back to that old cliche, the league table will mean nothing when the game begins and Liverpool’s Head Coach knows it only too well.

There will come a point when United leave their desperate form behind and Iraola, who could do with winning this contest after high-profile defeats to Arsenal and Manchester City, Isn’t being kidded by results after 10 games.

“United finished third in the table last season,” Iraola pointed out. “You are looking at a squad with exactly the same players. They had very, very good results, especially in the second half of the season. Now we have just started, this is just 10 games. So, for sure, they will be a lot higher in the table (soon). We have to rate them like this and the truth is the reference we have is that they finished third.”

The key to success for Liverpool will be winning the midfield battle and Dominik Szoboszlai - whose form has been up and down - needs to recapture his best.

Bruno Fernandes says he has shelved talks over a new contract because it is not the “right moment” for discussions over his future as Manchester United captain.

Fernandes, 32, is out of contract next summer although United have a 12-month option to extend his deal to 2028.

The Portugal midfielder is understood to have rejected two contract offers from United since the summer but said all his focus needs to be on trying to help the team out of their current plight.

United head into Sunday’s game against Liverpool at Anfield second from bottom in the Premier League.

“We spoke about the contract at the end of last season,” Fernandes told Sky Sports.

“We came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side because I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.

“The most important thing now is that the club gets back to winning games.”

Fernandes said claims he wants more money or a longer-term deal on offer are incorrect and that if finances were the issue he would have left Old Trafford before now. The captain has previously rejected lucrative offers from Saudi Arabia.

“The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay,” he said.

“There’s no negotiations ongoing, but I’ve seen people saying that ‘He’s asked for more money, he’s asked for more years’. If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here.

“I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.

“Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here.

“The thing is, I’ve always showed how much I care about the club and how much I want to win at this club. And I always said, in the moment the club thinks it’s time for me to move on, I will move on.

“I’m not going to be the player that I’ve seen many in this time at Manchester United. They’re going to stay here just by staying, just finish my contract and then we will see. In the moment the club says, ‘Bruno, it’s time to part ways’, I’m going to be the first one walking out the door.”

United chief executive Omar Berrada said of Fernandes on Friday that it was “true that we’re having conversations about his new contract” but that the club preferred “to keep that private”.

Having been voted PFA Player of the Year last season, Fernandes’ form has dropped off this term like that of the team.

He was dropped for the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth in the wake of a 4-1 drubbing by Como when he criticised the tactics and approach of then head coach Michael Carrick.

Mauricio Pochettino, Carrick’s successor, confirmed on Friday that Fernandes would remain as captain.

Fernandes said the United fans had been “far too patient with us” and hopes Pochettino - who wanted to bring the Portuguese to Spurs in 2019 - will bring a fresh energy.

“He’s someone that likes to bring a very good energy to the team, someone very positive, very strong, strict, said it straight away that he won’t allow us to not give him what he demands from the team, from each player,” Fernandes said.

“He wants the club to succeed so much, he wants to win games, and that’s pretty clear and obvious by the way he and his staff speak and want us to improve.

#928. 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?

Three artists share their thoughts on the reunification of East and West Germany. How do they perceive a shared "we" and what gives them cause for optimism?

When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.

Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.

Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.

In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.

The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

"November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

"The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a new one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalled. "I think it was just too fast for people."

The people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Western Pomerania, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home."

Today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany's most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.

"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

At the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in Feuchtenberger: "I soon realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very quickly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalled. "That made me afraid."

Meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As Menner put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.

In his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid."

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an issue that deeply concerns Menner — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.

His photo book "Top Secret" (2012, from publisher Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Some are eerie, while others are curious or even absurd.

Menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success," he said.

In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany's past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

Streisand believes literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she said. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened."

Interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

The story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.

The artist said she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West."

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she said. At the same time, it was a civic duty.

Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, said Feuchtenberger.

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than Menner, from West Germany.

"In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," said Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical issues, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he added, referring to the recent election successes of far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future."

"It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," said Feuchtenberger.

"For me personally, the whole issue of borders has somehow dissolved," she explained. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world.

Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border. "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want," she said. That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny."

"This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," said Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant."

This article was originally written in German.

#927. Why wasn't Szoboszlai's free-kick ruled out vs Man Utd?

Dominik Szoboszlai sparked Liverpool's rout of Man Utd with a free-kick goal after Leny Yoro was sent off, but should it have stood? United head coach Mauricio Pochettino believes Bradley Barcola was interfering with their defensive wall, although Bruno Fernandes appeared to push him

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Mauricio Pochettino fumed over Leny Yoro's red card for Manchester United in their defeat to Liverpool, but also felt Dominik Szoboszlai's opener should not have stood – is he right?

Yoro's one-match suspension for the red card he received in the 4-0 defeat at Anfield has been overturned, despite referees' chief Howard Webb supporting the decision to send him off.

But Szoboszlai's goal from the free-kick Yoro conceded in the same incident was allowed to stand, with Pochettino believing it should have been disallowed because Liverpool winger Bradley Barcola was interfering with the Man Utd wall.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The IFAB Laws of the Game state: "If, when a free-kick is taken, an attacking team player is less than 1m (1yd) from a 'wall' formed by three or more defending team players, an indirect free-kick is awarded."

Pochettino referenced a similar decision last season when Eberechi Eze's goal from a free-kick for Crystal Palace at Chelsea was disallowed after ex-Palace captain Marc Guehi pushed Moises Caicedo to create a gap for the ball to fly through.

Pochettino said: "No one talks about that the goal wasn't legal, it should be disallowed because (Bradley) Barcola was touching our wall.

"Maybe in the last two years, they've changed the rule because I've been in America, but last season when (Eberechi) Eze scored for Palace (at Chelsea) you can see [it was disallowed].

"But VAR didn't check [Dominik Szoboszlai's goal]; that must be disallowed."

When Szoboszlai strikes the free-kick, Barcola is clearly within 1m of the United wall and, under the Laws of the Game, the goal should be ruled out.

However, a key difference between Eze's disallowed goal and Szoboszlai's free-kick is that Guehi shoves Caicedo and moves within 1m of the Chelsea wall, whereas Bruno Fernandes appears to push Barcola towards the Man Utd defenders.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

In this case, it could be argued that Fernandes created the issue and Barcola ended up next to the Man Utd wall only because of his opponent's actions. The Laws of the Game do not provide an explanation for an attacker being pushed towards the defending team's wall.

VAR checks every goal and would have to decide whether it was a 'clear and obvious' error. Eze's goal was disallowed after the VAR had recommended a review to the referee over Guehi's involvement.

Another consideration is that Fernandes' push occurred before Szoboszlai struck the free-kick, meaning the ball was not in play, so it would not have been a foul by the United captain.

Had the referee spotted the push in the seconds before the free-kick was taken, he could have delayed the set-piece, disciplined Fernandes and then restarted from the original position.

Webb did not analyse the incident on the latest episode of Match Officials Mic'd Up.

Sky Sports News asked Pro Ref for comment.

Did Mauricio Pochettino throw Matthijs de Ligt to the Anfield wolves in order to make a point to the Manchester United hierarchy?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mauricio Pochettino barely had his feet under the table at Old Trafford - or rather, Anfield - on Sunday, but there he was throwing a teamsheet curveball into one of the biggest fixtures in the Manchester United calendar.

Starting Matthijs de Ligt was bold, to say the least, given the Dutchman had been out injured for such an extended period.

From the first minute, he looked every bit like a player who'd missed a large chunk of the past 12 months. Sky Sports co-commentator Gary Neville likened De Ligt's rustiness to his own return from a year out injured, after which he said he felt like he'd 'had six pints'.

Against a Liverpool side that presses relentlessly and isolates defenders, De Ligt looked heavy-legged from the first whistle. He was caught flat-footed on the turn, half a yard late to second balls, and spun humiliatingly by Alexander Isak in the immediate build-up to Leny Yoro's sending off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity.

You don't need your coaching badges to know what happens when you throw a rusty centre-half into that kind of intensity. Which begs the obvious question: did Pochettino do it on purpose?

Rarely do football managers strut into press conference and declare, "Half of this squad isn't fit for purpose, go and buy me new players." Not if they want to keep the dressing room on side, anyway.

With January around the corner and United still languishing in the bottom three, putting an undercooked De Ligt straight into the firing line felt like a very public memo aimed at the directors' box.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Had Pochettino packed the midfield, sat deep and ground out a respectable, low-event defeat, the hierarchy might have convinced themselves this group only needed minor tweaks in the winter window.

But, by rolling out an obviously flawed XI and letting the inevitable play out in real time in Sky Sports' prime Super Sunday slot, Pochettino stripped away any illusions. Every time De Ligt was left scrambling back towards his own goal, the argument for serious squad surgery in January effectively made itself.

Across his spells at Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea, Pochettino was never shy about subtly nudging club owners when he felt his squad lacked depth or physical conditioning, letting results and personnel headaches do the talking ahead of a transfer window.

Maybe that's giving him too much credit for dark arts, of course. Pochettino has always been obsessive about physical standards, and there's a world where he simply wanted to throw his biggest names into the deep end to see who actually has the stomach for a scrap. Although, when your backline is already patched together, picking a senior international - even one running on fumes - can look like the lesser of two evils.

Still, Pochettino has been around the block too many times to be naive about what Liverpool do to half-fit defenders. Whether it was calculated boardroom politicising or sheer necessity, chief executive Omar Berrada and technical director Jason Wilcox got an eyeful. There is much for them to think about ahead of January, because they cannot think that appointing the Argentine before dusting off their hands will suffice.

#925. Norway's ice hockey team says Russia replacing it at World Juniors

The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a "boycott."

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," said Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

"We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

Mikel Arteta is still king in the Premier League, with rivals struggling with intensity

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

‘Intensity’ is the buzzword of the moment, capturing a vibe that is just so Premier League.

For armchair tacticians - in particular for those pundits who lack the capacity for tactical analysis but know they ought to have this sort of thing down - ‘intensity’ is a usefully amorphous concept to deploy; the kind of word you can drop into a list alongside ‘leaving too much space’ and ‘nobody closing down’ and call it punditry.

‘Intensity’ is hard to define because it sits at the cross-section between pressing systems and the psychological. Does a high-intensity midfield press invigorate players to believe in their own mental intensity, or do the players need to feel the intense high-confidence of a high-intensity coach to engage their pressing intensity? It’s almost as if the word has no meaning.

But the application of the word ‘intensity’ across the Premier League weekend just gone can be instructive. Chelsea haven’t got it. Nor do Manchester City. Tottenham Hotspur have it. Liverpool have got it, sometimes, and Arsenal – Arsenal always have it, even if a lot of people don’t want to see it.

If there is a serious tactical point to be made here, it’s about the Premier League as a fast and direct division and - although it might sound sacrilegious to say it – it’s about Pep Guardiola’s modern irrelevance.

The great man himself foresaw this years ago, when he famously mused that “modern football is not positional”, and is instead being defined by “riding the rhythm” like Bournemouth.

Only one of his disciples listened, the one who looks set to win back-to-back Premier League titles. The others are floundering.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Enzo Maresca and Xabi Alonso are both students of Guardiola, the former his assistant at Manchester City and the latter a mentee when playing under Pep at Bayern Munich. Both managers historically prefer very low-tempo possession football (in their title-winning season, Alonso’s Bayer Leverkusen had the slowest direct speed upfield in the Bundesliga, at 1.71 m/s), a hallmark of Guardiola’s suffocating tactical domination of English football across seven years.

But the era of Guardiola ended more than two years ago. Watching Chelsea and Man City play this season, it shows.

Chelsea’s 4-1 defeat to Leeds United followed a pattern of the campaign, in that Alonso’s side appear too soft, steady, and meticulous in their actions to cope with the Premier League’s physicality. Alonso’s rigid ‘positional play’ – demarcated positions, sideways passing, detailed instructions of where each pass should go – is pure Pep. It simply could not cope with Leeds’ man-to-man pressing.

The Premier League is a fast and direct division… the era of Guardiola ended more than two years ago

Leeds recorded more recoveries (51 to 39) and more pressures (508 to 416) than Chelsea, had a considerably lower PPDA (13 to 19) and forced twice as many high turnovers (15 to 7). Yes, Leeds had intensity; Chelsea did not.

Over at the Etihad, it was startling to see the hosts refuse to press Fulham’s defenders at all, instead sitting in a quiet midblock that allowed Alvaro Arbeloa’s side to build momentum. From this low-intensity starting position, City could not engage quickly when Fulham sprung a counter-attack.

Looking at the arc of history, we are currently between eras, perhaps, with Andoni Iraola and Roberto De Zerbi – now there’s intensity – likely to emerge as major players once Long Guardiola fades and “riding the rhythm” takes its place. But in the meantime, Arsenal are in dynasty territory thanks to Mikel Arteta, a Guardiola disciple who cast aside his tutor’s teachings long ago.

He is not given anywhere near enough credit for this.

On Saturday, sloppy mistakes are all that prevented Arsenal from seeing out a brilliantly masterminded victory at St James Park, where Arteta’s tactical instructions pulled the man-to-man Newcastle press out of shape, creating ‘artificial transitions’: build-up attacks that, by baiting a press and then turning it, give the illusion of a counter-attack.

Time and time again, Kai Havertz would pull short as the false nine to drag a centre-back with him, at which point Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke would make clever inverted runs into the space for longer Arsenal passes to hit. It was fast, sharp, and intense – and it led directly to both goals.

It was seriously smart, out-witting Matthias Jaissle’s ‘high-intensity’ football (from the Red Bull school) and proving, again, that Arteta is one of the best tacticians the Premier League has ever seen.

That is not a popular opinion, probably because people do not like the conservatism that has increasingly defined Arsenal’s attacking play, but also because the tactical complexity of what he does – the form of ‘intensity’ his football takes – does not conform to expectations.

Accusations of low intensity are generally a wishy-washy way of saying the plan isn’t working, highlighting a tactical problem without actually defining what it is. But in the cases of Alonso and Maresca, it is easy to diagnose once we watch Arsenal’s verticality, their directness, their urgency in picking apart Newcastle’s game plan.

As usual, Arteta is ahead of the curve, and he comes with a message for Alonso and Maresca: if you want to play with ‘intensity’, you must first let go of the master’s teachings.

Alex Keble is a freelance football journalist based in London, specialising in tactical analysis. He has written for BBC Sport, Goal, The Mirror, The Independent, Football 365, and many others. As well as covering Premier League football, Alex works as a child therapist.

Six months after the glory of that Europa League final, Aston Villa’s return to Istanbul proved a chastening night of disappointment.

Unai Emery’s team have undergone a significant rebuild since that stirring night in May and this was another occasion where Villa 2.0 were exposed as a work in progress.

Emery’s run without a win has extended to six matches in all competitions and Villa’s Champions League campaign does not promise to get any easier, with Paris St-Germain up next.

There was always likely to be a period of transition this season, as six of the heroes from the Europa League final’s starting XI were sold over the summer.

Despite some encouraging signs before the last international break, and three successive Champions League wins, Villa are now enduring a difficult run.

Their second-half performance in particular was poor, and Galatasaray secured victory with the evening’s first shot on target.

The deadlock is FINALLY broken 🙌 Deniz Gül gives Galatasaray the lead after a scramble in front of the net. 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SplkgZC63p

Emery was booked late on as his frustrations got the better of him. His team appear short of creativity and, when Nicolas Jackson struggles, are toothless in the final third.

Though Villa did frustrate the Turkish champions for long periods on a slow, substandard pitch, this was a second successive defeat in the Champions League. Emery now faces a daunting double-header against PSG and Borussia Dortmund. They may still have enough to qualify for the knockout stages, but Villa fans of a certain vintage will insist their team never do it the easy way.

Emery was unhappy with the performance of German referee Daniel Siebert and said: “I am disappointed a little bit. After their goal, it was impossible to play. They wasted time. They added only five minutes. OK, finish the match. We don’t want to play more, I don’t think the referee was fair there. Two years ago we lost to Brugge and Monaco away [in the Champions League]. Today I can compare this match to those matches.”

Alejandro Garnacho, the Chelsea loanee, did not travel and was absent from the match-day squad for the fourth game in a row. Emery said: “Today the players were here who I think are the best players to be here with us.” It was far removed from the magical scenes of the Europa League showpiece across the city.

Villa’s fears before kick-off centred on the playing surface, with the pitch recently relaid after extensive maintenance, but it had no real impact on the result. Galatasaray defeated Liverpool twice in the Champions League at Rams Park last season and can be awkward opponents.

In a game of few chances, Villa were intent on frustrating both Galatasaray’s players and supporters by slowing the game down, restricting the home team’s threat by playing five in defence.

Galatasaray were lacking inspiration but were given an injection eight minutes into the second half. The flashpoint came after a crude challenge from Davinson Sánchez on Villa’s Brazilian winger Alysson.

Sánchez, the former Tottenham defender, escaped a booking but an angry John McGinn responded by colliding with Aleksey Batrakov near the touchline. Both players were given yellow cards by Siebert, and McGinn was infuriated that Batrakov avoided more extreme punishment for kicking out at him.

That aggravation only served to fire up Galatasaray and there was a sense of inevitability to their goal 13 minutes from the end. Villa were under pressure and failed to clear a corner, with Deniz Gul punishing Jackson’s error to head the ball over the line after a deflection off Tyrone Mings.

Seven minutes of added time failed to spark Villa into life by creating a late chance and they returned home without registering a shot on Ugurcan Cakir’s goal.

Villa’s downturn in form continues with a Champions League defeat which owed everything to their shortcomings going forward. They settled well in a hostile atmosphere, but allowed all their possession to drift into sterility, and the second half was just plain poor. A low-quality game settled by a messy goal, but credit to Gul for putting his head where it hurts.

Villa will surely finish the week outside the top eight, with home games against PSG and Borussia Dortmund to follow.

The referee has allowed the game on beyond the five additional minutes, but a Harwood-Bellis loose pass stalls Villa in their own half.

They soon break out into midfield space though, but with all the time in the world Barkley’s pass was a touch behind Hemmings and Sanchez was able to get a toe to it.

Of all the venues in the Champions League where a referee might be inclined to blow his whistle as soon as possible, this might be the one so time is running out for Villa.

Lucas Torreira has taken a kick on the ankle, and he limps off to be replaced by Ilkay Gundogan, who has played just 75 minutes this season.

Villa then find some space down the left but Singo blocks Maatsen’s cross which was aimed towards Jackson.

Ross Barkley the fourth Villa player booked on the night. There will be five minutes added on, which surely does not represent all of the stoppages, but Uefa’s approach to timekeeping resembles freestyle jazz.

Villa eventually worked a position to cross the ball from that free-kick, but Lindelof’s header back into the six-yard box was too close to Cakir and the goalkeeper pounced on the ball. Time running out for Villa.

Villa have been sleepwalking to defeat throughout the second half, they have completely lost any assurance in their passing game. That was better, and Goretzka wins a free-kick in midfield which they are going to clip forward.

Buendia has been brought on for Kamara, but Hemmings shoots over when Singo was on the turf appealing for a foul not given. Villa have shown more intent in the last three minutes than the previous 30.

The goalscorer Gul is back on with a bandage around part of his face.

Things could have gone from bad to worse for Aston Villa because VAR checked for a Jackson red card for a high boot on Gul, but eventually the incident is cleared. Villa have 10 minutes plus stoppage time to salvage a result.

Mbaye with a dangerous ball into the box but he was offside in any case.

Villa undone from a corner, and the striker thrown on as a substitute has scored the game’s opening goal. Gul appears to have hurt himself in the process, he took a kick in the face from Jackson when planting his head on the ball. Villa lost the first contact at the near-post and from there it was a mess. Gul receiving treatment with blood streaming down his face.
