#772. Vote for the first BBC Men's Footballer of the Year

Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.

Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.

The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.

The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.

Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.

"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.

"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."

The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.

The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).

Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.

Sorry, this vote cannot be loaded. In order to vote you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

Meet the SPOTY Men's Footballer of the Year contenders

Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.

In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.

That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.

Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.

The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.

Bellingham was recently joined in the England squad by his brother Jobe

In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.

His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.

Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.

Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.

Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.

Kane scored his first England goal 79 seconds into his debut in 2015

Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.

The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.

Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.

It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.

Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.

He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.

Mbappe has won eight consecutive league golden boots

Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.

By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.

His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.

Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.

His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.

Rodri scored the goal that won Manchester City the Champions League in 2023

Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.

Just days after his 19th birthday, the Spaniard became the youngest footballer to have played in - and won - both a World Cup and a European Championship. The only players younger than him to play in a World Cup final are Brazil's Pele in 1958 and Giuseppe Bergomi for Italy in 1982.

For the second year running, his performances led to a podium place at the Ballon d'Or and at the same award ceremony he became the first footballer in history to win the Young Talent of the Year three years in succession.

At club level, he was named La Liga's Best Player courtesy of a starring role in Barcelona's title success. The teenager ended the season with an impressive 24 goals and 18 assists across all competitions.

He recently broke Kylian Mbappe's record for the most goals by a teenager in Champions League history.

Lamine Yamal was 16 years and 362 days when he scored at the European Championship in 2024

#771. Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling

Sadio Mane's Senegal have been confirmed as Afcon 2025 winners following their appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, giving the Teranga Lions a second continental title

Senegal have been reinstated as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations after a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

The court's award overturns a previous decision which had stripped the West Africans of the title they won on the pitch during a chaotic final against host nation Morocco in January.

With the game goalless, Senegal left the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them. The match in Rabat was delayed by over 15 minutes before Morocco's Brahim Diaz had his spot-kick saved.

Senegal then triumphed 1-0 after extra time, with Pape Gueye scoring the winner.

That result was overturned almost two months later when a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board decreed the Teranga Lions had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play after the penalty was awarded.

Senegal's football federation (FSF) subsequently appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), sport's highest legal authority, with a three-man panel hearing its case behind closed doors in Lausanne on 8 October.

In a unanimous verdict, the Cas panel has effectively backed the decision by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala to restart the game after Senegal returned to the field and the match was played to a conclusion. The result of the final stands and Senegal are now confirmed as Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) 2025 winners.

A statement issued by Cas said the court considered that "the referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority".

"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume."

The FSF immediately reacted with a social media post featuring a picture of the side lifting the trophy in January captioned with the phrase "again and always champions of Africa".

"The FSF welcomes this ruling with deep satisfaction," it later said in a statement.

"This decision affirms, above all, the triumph of sporting fairness and reaffirms a fundamental principle: the true outcome of a match is determined exclusively on the field of play, under the protection of sports law."

Meanwhile, Morocco's football federation (FRMF) expressed "surprise" at the ruling and added that it would "pursue all available legal avenues to challenge the decision".

Caf says it respects the Cas award and "will take all the necessary measures to implement it".

The full grounds for the decision will be published by Cas in due course unless the parties request confidentiality.

'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Afcon 2025 final

'The longest VAR check in history' - the fallout from shock Afcon decision

Senegal's walk-off during the final in Rabat has already brought about a change in football's rules.

"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at â a âreferee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, in April.

"This new rule will also apply âto any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match âto be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."

Morocco and Senegal have both changed coach since the Afcon 2025 final and earlier this month secured their places at the 2027 edition of the tournament with two rounds of qualification remaining.

Referee Ndala was at the centre of the controversy during the Afcon final

A tightly contested final between the continent's top-ranked sides produced two moments of controversy in second-half stoppage time, with referee Ndala at the centre of the drama.

First the Congolese official denied Senegal a near-certain goal, blowing his whistle for a challenge by Abdoulaye Seck on Morocco right-back Achraf Hakimi moments before Ismaila Sarr nodded in.

The free-kick looked soft, but the video assistant referee (VAR) was unable to get involved because Ndala had awarded the foul before the ball crossed the line.

Three minutes later came a flashpoint in the Senegal box, when El Hadji Malick Diouf tugged Morocco playmaker Diaz back before heading a corner clear.

Diaz vehemently claimed a penalty and Ndala eventually awarded a spot-kick after being sent to consult his pitchside monitor by the VAR.

Senegal coach Pape Thiaw called his players over to the touchline, and Thiaw subsequently headed down the tunnel to the changing room in protest against the decision - accompanied by several players.

They eventually returned, but over 15 minutes had elapsed since the award of the penalty by the time Real Madrid's Diaz failed to convert, with his Panenka-style attempt easily saved by goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.

Meanwhile, there was unrest inside the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium as a small contingent of Senegal supporters clashed with security staff.

The game went into extra time, with midfielder Gueye scoring the goal which settled the contest in Senegal's favour.

Off the pitch, another match involving disciplinary boards and lawyers would soon begin.

Brahim Diaz's penalty was saved by Edouard Mendy after Senegal's walk-off led to a delay of over 15 minutes before he was able to take the spot-kick

Senegal celebrated their second continental title but the FRMF quickly lodged an appeal with Caf, arguing their opponents had breached Article 82 of Afcon regulations, which covers withdrawals.

It states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".

A disciplinary board from the continental game's governing body rejected the FRMF's appeal days after the final as it sanctioned and fined those found guilty of unsporting conduct during the match.

Yet in March, almost two months on from the final, a Caf appeals board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.

The FSF described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and swiftly lodged its case with Cas.

The director general of the Switzerland-based court said arbitration proceedings would be conducted "as swiftly as possible", but it was over five months until all parties descended on Lausanne for a one-day hearing.

The Cas panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.

Both the FRMF and FSF were able to nominate an arbitrator to exercise an independent judicial function once their appointment was confirmed.

The FRMF nominated Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli, while the FSF nominated Hamburg-based attorney and professor of âlaw at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas. Those two men completed the Cas panel.

Over six weeks on from that hearing - and 10 months since the Afcon 2025 final - Senegal have been proclaimed champions once again.

But the debate and damage done to the reputation of African football is likely to linger for some time yet.

In its appeal, the FSF argued that the decision of referee Ndala to resume the match in the 19th minute of added time - and to allow it to be concluded with a sporting result - could not be reviewed, pursuant to the 'field of play' doctrine.

Cas has a long-standing practice where it refrains from "reviewing decisions taken on the playing field by referees for applying the rules of the game, unless there is evidence that those rules were applied arbitrarily or in bad faith".

The FRMF argued, on the contrary, that the referee's decision did not fall under the field of play doctrine because Senegal should have faced disciplinary consequences for walking off the pitch.

The Moroccan federation went on to argue that, according to Afcon tournament rules, the referee should have brought the match to an early conclusion.

It added that Ndala "erred in law" and that his decision was "arbitrary".

However, in the view of the panel, the referee's decisions were limited to the pitch and the relevant Afcon regulations regarding withdrawals were not applicable.

"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," the Cas statement added.

"However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary'. On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."

Court of Arbitration for Sport reinstates Senegal as Afcon winners

Despite Cas being the highest authority in sport, and its decision coming 10 months on from the final, there could yet be a further twist.

The FRMF raised a grievance with the process before the panel's judgement was announced on Tuesday.

It alleged that German attorney Haas, the arbitrator on the panel nominated by the Senegalese, held a telephone call with FSF president Abdoulaye Fall on Sunday.

Fall "categorically" denies that any such phone call ever took place.

The FRMF says that any unauthorised communication between a member of the panel and one of the interested parties would constitute a serious breach of Cas regulations.

It has demanded that "appropriate legal consequences be applied to actions that compromise the integrity and credibility of the arbitration process".

The Moroccans could appeal against the ruling by taking the case to the Swiss Federal Tribunal, and the country's highest court could set Cas' judgement aside.

The case would then likely be heard again at Cas, with a different panel in place.

A precedent would be the case of Chinese swimmer Sun Yang, who had an appeal against the decision by Cas to impose an eight-year doping ban upheld by the Swiss Federal Tribunal.

A new panel heard his case at Cas, and his ban was reduced to four years and three months.

#770. How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

The scale of the economic disruption caused by AI has led even conservative politicians to talk about universal basic income. But economists aren't convinced, and campaigners think we need to ask deeper questions.

At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring 2025, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently."

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world.

This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socioeconomic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market."

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the nonprofit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of universal basic income (UBI).

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play."

The idea of a universal basic income is very old: English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances they said AI would bring.

In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable. Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But Herrmann said it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She isn't convinced that organizations like hers and people Elon Musk want the same thing.

"On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens."

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea.

Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living."

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at the University of Oxford and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible."

Kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he wrote. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history, partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact.

AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socioeconomic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she put it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?"

This, she argued, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work. "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," said Herrmann . "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?"

#767. Wales and West Ham's Morgan suffers serious injury

Ffion Morgan joined West Ham from Bristol City in 2025

Wales and West Ham winger Ffion Morgan is facing a lengthy spell on the sidelines after suffering an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury.

Morgan has undergone surgery having been helped off during West Ham's Women's Super League win over Charlton earlier this month.

The 26-year-old is now likely to miss the rest of the season.

"Ffion will now begin her rehabilitation programme under the supervision of the club's medical team," a West Ham statement said.

The injury also makes Morgan a major doubt for next summer's Women's World Cup, should Wales qualify.

Rhian Wilkinson's side take on Norway in a two-legged play-off final next week as they bid to reach the tournament for the first time in the nation's history.

Morgan, who has 56 caps, is an international regular and would be a shoo-in for the Wales squad if fit.

Five return for Wales' World Cup play-off final

Home World Cup can inspire Wales' future stars

She joined West Ham on a two-year deal in 2025 after her contract at Bristol City expired.

Morgan has also played for Cardiff City, Coventry United and Crystal Palace.

She suffered an ACL injury while playing for Wales Under-19s as a teenager, while she had only recently returned to action for West Ham after another lengthy fitness lay-off.

Wales face Norway at the Cardiff City Stadium on Tuesday, 1 December, before the return leg in Oslo four days later.

Wales are hoping to cause an upset as they bid to reach the Women's World Cup for the first time, though beating former champions Norway may not be enough to guarantee a place in Brazil next summer.

The complex nature of the qualification process means that Wales may have to negotiate inter-confederation play-offs next February to secure a World Cup place, even if they triumph over Norway.

#766. From sketch to publication-ready flowchart: how AI tools can bridge the gap

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Ensar Aydemir is an endocrinologist at Sultan 1. Murat State Hospital in Edirne, Türkiye. X: @dreaydemir

Artificial-intelligence tools can speed up the process of generating publication-ready flowcharts. Credit: -MG-/Getty

When making a scientific diagram, whether I am outlining a clinical study, planning a flowchart or mapping a signalling pathway, I often start in the same way: with a pen and a piece of paper.

Sketching by hand is fast. I can draw a box, cross something out and reorganize a whole idea without thinking about fonts, alignment or software menus. At this stage, my aim is not to make the figure beautiful, it is to work out the logic.

Turning that rough sketch into a clean figure for a manuscript can be surprisingly tedious, however. Text boxes need to line up; arrows need to connect properly; and fonts, spacing and colours must be consistent. A diagram that took five minutes to draw might take an hour or longer to recreate digitally.

Multimodal artificial-intelligence tools can shorten this process. Rather than asking an AI model to create the final scientific image, I use it as a translator. The model reads my sketch, interprets its structure and converts it into editable diagram code that I can open in a vector-based editor, such as Draw.io — a free application for making diagrams.

This distinction matters. I do not want AI to invent a figure for me; I want it to help me to digitize a figure that I have already designed.

One tempting approach is to provide a description to an image-generation model and ask for a polished scientific figure.

For research diagrams, this can create more problems than it solves. Text might be misspelt, arrows misdirected and pathways altered. More importantly, the resulting image is usually flat (that is, the text, images and background are merged together), making it mostly uneditable. For diagrams in research publications, if a reviewer later asks you to alter it, you might have to start from scratch.

A better option is to ask a multimodal language model — for example, Google’s Gemini — to turn your idea into a structured diagram format, such as Draw.io-compatible XML or Mermaid syntax. The output can then be imported into a diagram editor, in which every box, label and connector remains editable.

In this workflow, AI is less an illustrator than a compiler: a programming tool that translates human-readable instructions into code that a computer can run. My sketch is the source, and Draw.io XML is the output.

Focus first on the structure of your figure. I roughly sketch the important nodes, branches and connections without worrying about visual polish. For a clinical study, these might include eligibility criteria, treatment groups and follow-up visits. For a laboratory workflow, they might represent experimental stages or decision points.

The key is to make the relationships clear. What box comes first? Where does the pathway split? Which arrow connects to which endpoint? If the logic is ambiguous to a human reader, it will be ambiguous to the AI model, too.

Once the sketch is complete, I photograph it, upload the image to a vision-enabled language model and provide a detailed prompt. For instance:

“Recreate the uploaded hand-drawn figure as a clean, editable academic flowchart in Draw.io-compatible XML format. Preserve the original structure as faithfully as possible, including box positions, arrows, dashed connectors, side boxes, branching pattern, and text content. This is a reconstruction task, not a redesign task. Use a plain white background, thin dark slate-grey borders, white box fills, thin connector lines, clean sans-serif text, and no shadows, gradients, or decorative elements. Make it publication-quality while keeping it recognizably the same diagram.”

The instruction “This is a reconstruction task, not a redesign task” is crucial. Scientific diagrams are not the place for creative completion. I want the model to reconstruct my structure, not improve it on my behalf.

Note also that this prompt indicates what the model should not change. I explicitly ask it to preserve wording, branching relationships and directionality. If the diagram contains important numbers, doses or time points, I check each one manually.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03513-1

#765. Violet Witchel Won’t Judge You for These Thanksgiving Dinner Shortcuts

Thanksgiving is practically here, and we turned to content creator and cookbook author Violet Witchel for some last-minute hosting tips, dinner shortcuts and more.

While we're getting ready to shop until we drop on Black Friday, let's not forget about what comes first: Thanksgiving. The holiday that's all about food and family can also come with a side of stress, especially if you're hosting.

We chatted exclusively with Violet Witchel, content creator and cookbook author, whose dense bean salads have totally transformed how I think about meal prepping for the week. And she came through with the best tips to help us with hosting, prepping food and even being a great holiday guest!

But if you're feeling stressed about your Thanksgiving menu and how you can get all the cooking and prep work done in time for dinner... don't be! Because guess what, even chefs like Violet pick up a few pre-made ingredients to help save time.

"Pre-made pie crust, mixes - like if you're going to make cornbread, get cornbread mix. Canned cranberry sauce, totally fine," she said of the items she'd get from the store. "Pre-bought stuffing, like the mix, totally fine. Pre-minced vegetables, totally fine."

But one thing you won't catch her using? Powdered mashed potatoes. "I think on Thanksgiving, you've gotta do that from scratch."

And whether you're team pumpkin, apple or pecan, supporting a local bakery is not only tasty but also a time-saver she added. Don't forget the canned whipped cream and your favorite ice cream!

For more food prep advice and tips from Violet, keep reading!

"I don't love to bring wine because I feel like everyone brings wine and they feel kind of obligated to serve it at dinner," Violet shared. "So I love to bring a nice bottle of olive oil because it's one of those things you're like 'oh, this is wonderful to have.' "

This duo by Brightland is on sale and ready for gifting! It includes the smooth and delicate Alive EVOO, the bold and robust Awake EVOO, two gold pouring spouts, and comes gift-ready in a 2026 holiday box.

As for something she's received as a gift while hosting that she loved, she shared: "Someone brought us a houseplant once, which was very fun. Flowers are one thing, but this plant has now lived in my office for years."

These lush pink and green leaves, available in a pot color of your choosing, on this Aglaonema cultivar, will thrive in a variety of light levels.

And for the person in your life that is always cooking, they should definitely have fresh herbs at home if they don't already. "I love basil, especially if you have a sunny window. I feel like basil can withstand anything," she shared.

Grow your own herbs at home! This kit comes with three basil pods and a grow light if you don't have a sunny window.

"You might not think a candle in the bathroom is a hosting essential, but it is," Violet said. "I love the Flamingo Estate candles. I think they're so chic, they burn forever, they smell so good. I love them."

Violet loves the "summery and earthy" scent of Flamingo Estate's Heirloom Tomato candle, which she says can go into fall or winter.

"An immersion blender is kind of my holy grail, I use that for everything. Pulling out a full food processor or blender is kind of an ordeal, but if you want to make a delicious, perfectly blended dressing, an immersion blender is so perfect for that."

This powerful and versatile immersion blender by Ninja also comes with a Rapidwhisk attachment, that you can operate with speed control. Plus, it's dishwasher-safe!

She also loves "a really, really sharp microplane or box grater, especially if you're making mac and cheese."

Efficiently zest citrus, grate cheese and more with a microplane that saves you time and energy while prepping.

This 4-sided box grater by OXO has a removable zester for handheld help, plus a comfortable soft handle, non-slip foot and removable clear container to keep food in place while you work.

Speaking of mac and cheese, she said that's her most-complimented recipe she's ever made. She even had a guest "ask for a to-go box" of it one time!

For more gluten-free recipes (yes, including dense bean salads) that will have your guests asking for seconds, pre-order Violet's upcoming debut cookbook!

More favorites include "a really good, sharp knife" and "a good, heavy cutting board."

Forged from a single piece of WÜSTHOF steel, it is made with forged half bolsters for balance and optimal weight, with an ergonomic handle that makes slicing and dicing a breeze.

When you're prepping a full holiday meal, you can't be slowed down by only having one cutting board on hand! This set of three from Caraway also comes with a storage organizer.

You're probably spending a lot on food, so you don't need to spend a ton on every kitchen tool, but one that Violet would splurge on is "a really great wooden salad bowl."

"It's very chic, if you take good care of it it's something you have forever," she added.

Ideal for salads and even mashed potatoes, this large wooden bowl has a gorgeous natural grain that adds organic appeal and visual texture to your tablescape.

"I do not splurge on napkins or tablecloths," she added. "You can dress it up with runners... I don't think anyone remembers the tablecloth."

Available in multiple colors and patterns, we love that this tablecloth has a ruffle detail along the edge for added intrigue.

These cloth napkins are made of 100% cotton, for a high-quality and plush feel.

#764. Millwall face partial stadium closure after discriminatory chants

Millwall, who are 16th in the Championship, have average league gates of 19,418 at The Den this season

Millwall have been ordered to play a future Championship match in front of a partially-closed stadium as punishment for fans' discriminatory chants.

The club has also been fined Â£70,000 by an independent regulatory commission, and been told another offence this season will lead to a further partial stadium closure.

The sanctions were imposed for ableist and homophobic chants, heard at a game against Charlton Athletic in January.

"These chants are discriminatory, unacceptable, and will not be tolerated at The Den or anywhere Millwall play," Millwall's managing director Mark Fairbrother said in an open letter to supporters., external

Anti-discriminatory body Kick It Out said it welcomed "greater accountability for discriminatory mass chanting".

Fairbrother said Millwall condemned the chants "without reservation".

"They do not represent this club, and the vast majority of supporters who follow Millwall home and away with passion and pride," he added.

"Incidents like this hurt all of us, but none more so than people who are directly discriminated against by ableist, homophobic or other unacceptable chanting, and we apologise to anybody that was affected, offended or impacted by the chants."

Blocks 19, 20, 47 and 48 of the Dockers Stand - the two-tiered east stand at The Den - will have to be closed for the Championship fixture against Sheffield United on 8 December.

It is the first time a club has been given this level of sanction for discriminatory chanting, with the commission saying "the club's previous disciplinary record was a significant aggravating feature".

The commission pointed to chants relating to race in a 2019 fixture against Everton, religion in a 2023 fixture away at Wigan Athletic, and sexual orientation and disability in a 2025 visit to Crystal Palace, all of which resulted in fines for the club.

"History has shown that combinations of action plans and fines have been wholly ineffective to prevent the club - through its supporters - committing breaches" of Football Association (FA) rules around discriminatory behaviour, the commission added.

The FA had charged Millwall in March for the chanting against Charlton.

The club admitted the charge, and in its submissions suggested the chants were limited to 80 to 100 individuals in the north-eastern corner of the Dockers Stand, in the blocks that will be closed as part of the punishment.

However, based on other evidence, the commission concluded the actual figure involved in the chants was "likely to have been in the hundreds, quite possibly more".

It also found that the club did not make any announcement over the stadium PA system ordering for the discriminatory chanting to stop, nor did it deploy any additional stewards or police to the areas from where the chanting was originating.

"I won't dress this up. This is a serious outcome," Fairbrother said.

"This significant sanction was given because, although this is the first charge relating to a match at The Den for many years, the commission took into account a number of incidents of discriminatory chanting involving our supporters over the past few seasons at away games.

"This is the cumulative cost of that pattern. Most importantly, the current and any future sanctions mean the next incident won't just cost the club money. It will cost supporters their seats.

"Innocent fans will be shut out of their own stadium because of someone else's behaviour, and with future sanctions likely to be tougher, that threat is very real."

In a statement, Kick It Out said it had received a record number of mass chanting reports across football last season, including racist, sexist and misogynistic, homophobic, ableist and faith-based abuse.

"Education has a key role here, both for fans, so that they know the impact and consequences of discriminatory chanting, and clubs, so they can proactively help to reduce its prevalence," the statement added.

"We stand ready to support football in helping eradicate this problem."

#760. Rylee Arnold's Boyfriend Posts Message on DWTS Finale With Connor Wood

Dancing With the Stars pro Rylee Arnold—partnered with influencer Connor Wood—shared how her boyfriend, Walker Lyons, supported their team ahead of the season 35 finale.

Rylee Arnold's boyfriend thinks Connor Wood is all that jazz.

After Wood addressed fans who hoped that his partnership with his Dancing With the Stars coach might translate off the dance floor, the pro's real-life match, BYU football player Walker Lyons, chimed in with support for the team taking home the season 35 title.

"Today is the day! So proud of you and the work you have put in to get here, so deserving," Lyons captioned a shot of Arnold holding a supersized bouquet of roses on Instagram Stories Nov. 24. As for the influencer known as Fibula, he added, "Vote for Connor."

And the 21-year-old treasured the romantic gesture from her boyfriend of two years, calling the floral display that arrived that morning, "the best surprise ever."

Wood, 31, previously tap-danced past speculation about his relationship with Arnold in a Nov. 10 TikTok Live, sharing one message for viewers wishing to turn his shot at the Mirrorball into fan fiction: "I say, 'Thank you for watching.'"

However, Arnold had plenty of words to express how much she valued finding a romance with Lyons.

"There were so many crazy coincidences that actually brought us together," she told E! News following the Halloween episode Oct. 30. "He’s just such a great guy, I really found a good one who makes me feel so special. And we have so much fun together."

The Dancing with the Stars: Juniors alum added regarding the attention around her onscreen chemistry with Wood that she told the 22-year-old, "'It's scary I know,'" noting how Lyons has been "the best sport about it—he’s just the best."

As such, Arnold didn't hold back when remarking how excited she was to find a platonic partner in crime in the podcaster for her fourth season as a pro.

"It just feels natural," Arnold told Entertainment Weekly in September. "I think naturally we just have so much fun together. We feel comfortable with each other."

But that doesn't mean all of the dancing duos on the ABC competition series stayed just pals. For more stars and pros who foxtrotted out of friendship on DWTS, keep reading...

The season 33 partners dated for about seven months between 2024 and spring 2025.

In April 2025, the fellow DWTS pros kissed on the lips onstage on the final night of the series' 2025 tour during their show-closing duet dance, confirming months of romance rumors.

Months after placing fifth in the 31st season of the dance show, the couple confirmed their romance on Valentine's Day 2023. "My Valentine," the CODA actor captioned a selfie with the choreographer. "Happy Valentine's Day!"

Stewart and Durant then announced their engagement in December 2023 and married in front of a trouple of DWTS pros in August 2025.

While she was partnered with Hayes Grier, the two hit it off during season 21's Switch Up Week, with Skarlatos calling the pro dancer "so hot." After her elimination, Slater teased that they two had yet to go on a date, saying, "We'll see."

Meanwhile, Skarlatos playfully told E! News, "No comment!"

The dance pro and Bachelorette alum were romantically linked while competing together on DWTS' season 33 in 2024. However, their offscreen chemistry fizzled out by June 2025 shortly after Tran returned to Miami to finish her master's degree.

Which bring us to these two. After dating a little on-and-off since 2011, the pros got engaged live on the show in October 2016 and were married in March 2018. However, E! News confirmed in August 2022 that Slater and Farber were going their separate ways after four years of marriage.

"It's not a nightmare at all," Slater told E! News. "We support each other so much that I want the very best for Sasha. We support each other, very, very truly."

Chmerkovskiy and Johnson were dating in 2015, before she was promoted to pro dancer. They got engaged in June of 2018 before making it official and walking down the aisle in April of 2019. The two welcomed son Rome Valentin in January 2023.

"Life is awesome," Chmerkovskiy told E! News in May 2023. Becoming a dad "definitely elevated my joy for life, my joy for my family, and every day I learn something new being a father."

In December 2020, E! News learned the Selling Sunset star was dating the Dancing With the Stars pro after they had competed separately on season 29.

However, after two months of dating, E! News exclusively confirmed they had called it quits. At the time, a source close to the realtor said, "They had a fun time together but in the end, decided it would be best if they part ways. They are still friendly and cordial. It wasn't a messy breakup, just wasn't the right fit or right timing."

Platonic throughout their seventh-place-finishing 2017 run, the Total Bellas star and the former Dancing With the Stars pro found their way back to each other after her split from John Cena in 2018. Garcia confirmed her relationship with Chigvintsev in May 2019, and they got engaged later that year.

The WWE Hall of Famer learned she was expecting soon after their Paris engagement, with them welcoming son Matteo Artemovich Chigvintsev in 2020.

Sadly, though, the pair are no longer partnering up. Garcia filed for divorce in September 2024, two weeks after Chigvintsev was arrested on suspicion of domestic violence. Ultimately, the Napa County District Attorney's office announced they decided not to file charges against him "after a thorough review of the criminal investigation and careful evaluation of the evidence presented to the DA’s Office."

The pair settled their divorce in November 2024, with Garcia's rep noting the two also dropped their "the domestic violence restraining orders against each other in an effort to move on with their lives and effectively co-parent their son."

The model and the relatively new pro flirted up a storm throughout season 27, and Ren had admitted on the show that she had a crush on him. At the time, a source even told E! News that they "really enjoy each other's company" and were "seeing where things go."

However, multiple outlets reported in December 2018 that the pair had split.

The professional dancers got engaged on Dec. 5, 2015, after dating since 2012. Maks proposed onstage at the SWAY: A Dance Trilogy event in Miami. Six months after welcoming their son Shai, the lovebirds exchanged vows during a lavish ceremony in July 2017. They then welcomed baby Rio in June 2023 and their third son Milan in July 2024.

The partners struck up a romance in season five, but broke up a few months after their shocking exit. Still, Bryan and Ballas remained friendly, with The Cheetah Girls star even returning to the ballroom to cheer for him the following season.

Funnily enough, the duo had gone out on several dates before he even signed up for the show. And while they denied any romance rumors during season 18, that didn't stop them from playing up their chemistry during performances.

Soon after the Shark Tank star announced he was separating from his wife of 14 years Diane Plese, sources confirmed to E! News that he and Kym Johnson, his pro partner from season 20, were dating and "really happy together."

While Robert and Kym at first played coy about the nature of their relationship, that quickly stopped. They were engaged in February 2016, married by June 2016, and welcomed twins in April 2018.

Partnered in season three, the Saved by the Bell alum quickly struck up a romance with the dance pro, which went on for two years before they called it off for good in 2008. "The relationship wasn't heading in the right direction," Smirnoff's rep said in a statement, after rumors of infidelity on Lopez's part.

The professional dancers got engaged in 2009 after six months of dating following her split from Mario Lopez. Sadly, they called it off later that same year. But the duo remained friendly, even going on vacations together.

Married since 2014, the pros announced the arrival of their daughter Nikita in May 2023.

Daniella shared the happy news by posting a photo and video of Pasha with Nikita to Instagram Stories. She wrote "daddy's girl" alongside the clip and "My Geminis" beside the picture.

After showing off their insane chemistry during the sixth season, the duo dated for nearly a year before announcing their 2009 breakup in the most cordial way ever: matching tweets! "Hi everyone, we wanted you all to know directly from us, that Shannon & I have decided to end our relationship as boyfriend & girlfriend...," Hough tweeted that August, with Elizabeth writing, "However, we love and care about each other very much and will remain friends and in each others lives."

Derek is now married to his dance partner Hayley Erbert.

#757. Dancing With the Stars Season 35 Winner Revealed After Major Comeback

DWTS crowned Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach the champions of season 35 during the nail-biting Nov. 24 finale after out-dancing Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins, Tatyana Ali and Connor Wood.

Dancing With the Stars’ new champion sprinted straight to the top.

During the season 35 finale, Ezra Frech and partner Daniella Karagach secured the Mirrorball Trophy after making an incredible recovery from a prosthetic mishap during their freestyle—making Frech the first Paralympian to take home the title.

And it's clear the pair found their rhythm, delivering show-stopping routines during the Nov. 24 episode. In addition to receiving perfect scores by judges Derek Hough, Carrie Ann Inaba and Bruno Tonioli, Ezra also becomes the first amputee to win the show and the youngest man to win at 21, besting last year's champ Robert Irwin.

"This is the most special moment of my life," Ezra shared. "Thank you, everybody, for voting. Thank you for believing in us. Oh my God."

Daniella—earning her second Mirrorball following her victory with Iman Shumpert in season 30—added, "I'm just so freaking grateful."

Of course, the 2026 champions achieving the sole purpose of the competition meant they outscored runner-up Amber Glenn, as well as Connor Wood, Tatyana Ali and Maura Higgins.

In a salsa danced to "Danza Kuduro," Ezra and Daniella set the stage on fire. To switch things up, the runner also landed an empowering freestyle to "Numb" by Linkin Park, which Daniella teased on the show's official podcast Nov. 19 would include moves that have "definitely never been done before," like Ezra beginning the routine without his prosthetic.

After putting on the device mid-routine, it unsuctioned later in the dance, but he was able to make an impressive recovery, with Derek raving, "The worst-case scenario might have happened and you wouldn't even have known, the way you rose in that moment."

Meanwhile, Amber and partner Pasha Pashkov moved their feet to a quickstep set to "Sing Sing Sing" by Louis Prima, complemented by a colorful freestyle to Madonna hits "Like a Prayer" and "Music."

Wood led pro Rylee Arnold in an emotional Viennese Waltz, in addition to a freestyle mashing up "Singin’ in the Rain" and Rihanna's "Umbrella." They were joined by Rylee's sister, Lindsay Arnold Cusick, for the routine after the former pro stepped away from the show in 2021.

Love Island's Higgins tangoed with Mark Ballas, then balancing out the spicy number with a jazzy rendition of "Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend" featuring Irish folk song selections as a nod to her heritage. And Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik delivered the night's third tango, as well as a jazzy freestyle to a Judy Garland song that was out of this world.

Amber, Ezra and Maura all received perfect scores of 90 while Connor and Tatyana received 82 points from the judges.

Still, all of the finalists were surrounded by support from their previously eliminated castmates taking one more spin around the ballroom. Their return reminded viewers of the year's shocking twists and turns that sent home top performers like Harry Shum Jr., Jenna Dewan and Taylor Hanson despite their consistently positive feedback from the judges' panel.

On the other foot, stars like Julia Stiles and Ciara Miller—whose claim to fame in the competition became their heartfelt connection with partners Ezra Sosa and Brandon Armstrong, respectively—delighted the audience by coming in all smiles following their emotional eliminations.

That said, while only one winner can take home the title, DWTS has changed the lives of many of its alums. Read on for more secrets about the ABC series.

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last."

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show."

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody."

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together."

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'"

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner."

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well."

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again."

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers."

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting."

#755. DWTS' Ezra Frech Makes Incredible Recovery After Prosthetic Falls Off

Dancing With the Stars contestant Ezra Frech pulled off a miraculous recovery after his prosthetic unsuctioned from his leg while performing his freestyle in the finale with Daniella Karagach.

Ezra Frech cha-cha'd real smooth past a mishap during the Dancing With the Stars finale.

The Paralympian and pro partner Daniella Karagach sent a powerful message with their freestyle routine to "Numb" by Linkin Park on the Nov. 24 finale, bringing in wheelchair users and professional dancers Joel Brown and Rafael Castellano as guest stars before taking home the Mirrorball trophy.

But it was also Frech's own flawless recovery that inspired audiences, as the 21-year-old began the poignant performance without his prosthetic leg before putting it on mid-show. However, it unsuctioned during the routine, forcing him to lift Karagach in the air while balancing on one leg.

After the stunning feat, Frech then smoothly reattached his prosthetic and nailed the rest of the choreography, earning perfect 10s from judges Derek Hough, Carrie Ann Inaba and Bruno Tonioli.

After cohost Alfonso Ribeiro confirmed Frech's "incredible recovery" was not pre-planned, Hough praised the athlete as a "hero."

"This performance will have a ripple effect far beyond this show. What you did tonight was forever," Hough said. "Kids will look up to you and see what's possible."

He noted, "The worst-case scenario might have happened, and you wouldn't even have known the way you rose in that moment."

Tonioli agreed, adding, "What we witnessed tonight goes beyond dancing. This is a powerful, beautiful, life-affirming statement that will inspire the nation and the world."

"The leg unsuctioned, and it came off in the middle of the dance," Frech explained. "But listen, we put our heart, our blood, our sweat, our tears into this."

He added, "If one person with a disability feels more confident and holds their head up high because of this show, then I've done my job."

That message of empowerment was the foundation of their performance, as Frech noted in the pre-taped package.

"I want it to be a celebration of what is possible when you're different," he told Karagach in rehearsal through tears. "What you've done, leaning into my prosthetic, finding such a beautiful way to highlight it and not shy away from it, is unbelievable."

For their last dance, they picked an anthem from Linkin Park that Frech said is "all about breaking stereotypes."

"No sob story. This is all about power," he explained. "We're going to be bringing high intensity with talented wheelchair dancers, because we want to change the way people see disability through this dance."

The number led to Frech and Karagach winning season 35, with him becoming the first Paralympian to take home the Mirrorball, as well as the first amputee and youngest male winner.

As Frech put it, "This is the most special moment of my life."
